questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted a historically and culturally rich destination, and Bologna fit that description perfectly. It was superbly located in the middle of Italy in one of the country's most interesting regions. I had, however, also heard good things about the university and was obviously aware of its position as the oldest university in Europe.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy, although a bit confusing. They sent me quite a lot of information on email, but it was a bit overwhelming to figure out the right order to do things. I guess that's more or less an inevitable part of it, so I was not too frustrated by it.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got some e-mails about check in, where to go to get my student card etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Extremely difficult. I was shocked by this, as I had expected to find housing easier. And it was a lot more expensive, than I thought it would be. I ended up paying more than in Copenhagen, and I had the cheapest housing compared to my friends down there. There is a literal housing crisis in Bologna right now, which resulted in lots of demonstrations and protests by the Italian students as well. They keep building new, fancy student housing around the city, but it's ridiculously expensive (like 800-900 euros a month) and you should not support these sites if possible. They only want to take advantage of desperate exchange students. My biggest recommendation is to start looking as early as possible, and be extremely cautious especially on Facebook groups, because 95% is scam. I found my housing through a friend who had lived there the year before, so I got lucky. And the biggest advice is just to not pay anything before you've actually seen the place and know it exists!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: That even though you may not end up in your dream housing, you will be just fine :)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really wish the University of Bologna took the crisis seriously and did something about it. They should really be ashamed of the situation right now, where they proudly present their university and facilities but offer no help with housing for exchange students.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Once I figured out which platform to use it was fairly simple. But the courses are not always public until very late in the process so a bit of patience was required for that. 

My absolute biggest issue with this process was the fact that I HAD to choose at least one course from a department that I really wasn't too interested in. For some reason I had been assigned to this department and they didn't have a lot of English courses of any relevance to my studies. I ended up finding something, which then turned out to be the worst course I've had in my life, but that's another story ...

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I emailed both professors and people at the exchange student desk who were quite helpful

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got everything I wanted but had to change things up a few times because of scheduling issues.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just ask for help when you need it. Otherwise it will be quite confusing.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: VERY mixed experiences with my courses. Some were great, some were beyond awful.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Almost all of my courses were on MA level, but I could easily follow them without difficulty. I would say that the level is generally lower than in Copenhagen, but the exam period is so intense because you have so many smaller courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Fairly similar. Some classes you would just sit and listen for two hours straight, but some professors were also interested in involving the students more, which I found great. I guess it all depends on the professor, just like it does here.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Visual Communication
Literature and Visual Culture 
Introduction to Italian Culture
Cultural Economics
Italian Pop Cultures

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Visual Communication was fantastic and easily had the best teacher I've had not only in Bologna, but probably during all my time in university. I highly recommend this course. It was relevant, up to date, inclusive and had a great mix of theoretical and practical learning. 

Italian Pop Cultures was also super interesting and I learned a lot in that course.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing of note, really. I just spent a lot more money on traveling, events, concerts, football games etc. than I expected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Housing was easily the most surprising part, as I had expected to pay around 3500 kr pr month. But food, drinks etc. are generally quite cheap down there.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I'm sure there were opportunities, but I did not make much of an effort to look into that. There was so much else to do constantly.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: In the city of Bologna, I would recommend reading up on what's happening in terms of events etc. There is literally some sort of festival happening every weekend. I watched quite a lot of films as well (they have an excellent cinematheque), I went to some of the museums, checked out all of the churches multiple times, saw Bologna FC 3 or 4 times (highly recommend, even if you're not a big football fan). You will neeeever be bored in Bologna!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
The region of Emilia-Romagna is full of incredible cities that can ALL be recommended: Modena, Parma, Cesena, Ferrara, Ravenna etc. I traveled a lot during the weekends, mostly just on one-day trips, where I watched a football game and saw a new city. It was so much fun and can be pretty cheap. The train connections are great from Bologna, and Flixbus has super cheap connections to popular destinations like Venezia, Firenze and Milano. 

I would also recommend going to the beach or visiting some nature, as Bologna is a bit intense and very "city-like".

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty straightforward, I think. I came for the cultural aspect so naturally I wanted to experience that as much as possible. People are kind and open in Bologna.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Not really, as I met very few local students. I did, however, meet loads of wonderful exchange students like myself through the Erasmus Student Network. It's a must that you sign up for this when you get there, they do tonnes of events every week and it's a great way to meet other people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Honestly probably just that a lot of stuff closes down for siesta and during Sundays/Mondays. Just be aware of that, and it won't be an issue at all. Just takes a little bit of getting used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The spontaneity of Italian people is so cool. They just get out there and do stuff. I really enjoyed that you could go for a cheap Aperol Spritz on a random Tuesday night without having to get absolutely plastered. I really found myself appreciating small things so much more down there.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Get out there and explore. Get lost in the city, find hidden gems and cool spots and just enjoy yourself. 
- Don't worry too much about money. It will ruin the experience if you do. Obviously, make sure you aren't running entirely out but you can always earn it again, when you come back. I'm just saying that you shouldn't say no or hold back because you don't want to spend too much money. This is a once in a lifetime experience, and if not now, then when? 
- It's okay to have a night by yourself at home as well! I did that many times, because you cannot be social every single day. Try to find a balance and don't worry about missing out on anything. There'll be so many opportunities during your semester.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I don't think so.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: That I got to eat great food, be in a beautiful city, meet fantastic people while studying. It's an experience I will never forget, and I'm SO happy I did it.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding the balance between studies and experiences. I had a hard time with this, especially in the beginning as I wanted to see and do so much all the time. Take your time and remember that you are also there to study :) And don't wait too long before you begin writing your exams. I did that and had a very hectic April/May/June.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
